newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel to complain to U.N. over PLO land law.
newsitem.headline: Israel to complain to U.N. over PLO land law.

text.p: Israel said on Wednesday it would complain to the U.N. committee on human rights over the Palestinian Authority's decision to impose the death penalty on people who sell land to Jews.

Meanwhile, a member of the Israel Lands Administration council and the deputy chairman of the quasi-governmental Jewish National Fund told Israel Radio that, despite a ban, there were Israelis who were selling land "back to the Arabs".
Peacemaking between the sides ground to a halt in March when Israel began building a new 6,500-home Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem.
A statement issued by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said:

"The cabinet secretary, who is also the chairman of the government forum following anti-Semitism worldwide, is about to present the U.N. committee on human rights with a complaint about the Palestinian Authority decision."
"The decision is in essence racist and reeks of anti- Semitism," it added.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in an interview published on Wednesday that he backed the recent decision to enforce an old Jordanian law in the West Bank imposing the death penalty for land sales to Jews.
"We are talking about isolated traitors," Arafat said. "And we will impose against them what is on the law books. That is our right and our obligation to protect our land."

Israel has linked the ban on land sales with the recent killings of two Palestinian land dealers found dead in the West Bank. The Authority, which says the law is applied by the courts and not vigilantes, has denied any involvement in the killings.
Haim Cohen, the Israeli lands official, told Israel Radio the Palestinan Authority was trying to buy land inside Israel.
"There is no doubt that there has been a large increase of offers to Jews. To our regret, we've also come upon situations in which Jews out of greed are ready to sell land back to Arabs," Cohen said.
He said in areas where Israeli law applied, it was against the law to sell land to foreigners.
"That is to say he would still need a permit if he is selling it to a foreigner, he still needs a permit from the State of Israel via the Administration," Cohen said.
Cohen said a subsidiary of the Jewish National Fund (JNF) owned most of the the land on which Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip sat.

"We are doing everything to encourage the continuation of Jewish settlement both inside and outside the Green Line," he said. "Green Line" refers to Israel's border before its capture of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in the 1967 Middle East war.

Cohen said that the JNF, in operation before Israel was established in 1948, owned large tracts of land in Palestinian Authority areas and in Jordan but that Israel so far had made no claims on those lands.
The Palestinians hope to establish a state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip with East Jerusalem, also captured in 1967, as its capital. They say settlement building pre-empts final status peace talks.
More than 130,000 Israelis have settled amid some two million Palestinians in the areas. The Authority hopes to stop settlement expansion with the stiff land law.
